extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evidentiary tests for determining patent infringement: when a second patent or product is distinct or is an infringement of a prior patent, including rules about combinations, proportions, mechanical equivalents, and colorable evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct subject-matter / independent patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after a patent has been obtained, another person by his own genius and discovery gives the public, without reference to or borrowing from the former one, a new and superior mode of arriving at the same end, there can be no objection to his taking out a patent for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new patent must be the author's own skill and labour and not 'a leaf out of his neighbor's book.' The test is whether the second patent is perfectly distinct from the former or is virtually bottomed upon it, varying only in immaterial circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement test — whether defendant added anything material
rubrics_metrics.description: The question as to the infringement is whether the defendants had added any thing material, not covered by the plaintiff's patent, which could be considered as constituting a subject-matter distinct from that of the plaintiff's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the materials, the mode of putting them together, and the operation/result. If differences are merely circuitous modes of doing what the patentee claimed, they may still infringe (example: caoutchouc cards where a circuitous method produced the same elasticity next to the teeth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorable imitation versus substantial difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A colorable imitation (mere variation in mode or form) that accomplishes the same principle and result as the plaintiff's patent may be infringement; conversely, a real and substantial difference in materials, construction or operation may support an independent patent and avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether differences are 'material' and 'substantial' (e.g., mechanical vs chemical process, different proportions, different end-effect). Evidence from practical and scientific witnesses may be decisive; juries determine fact questions of substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions/degree as part of the essence of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When proportions or degrees are specified as the mode in which a particular effect is to be produced, they make a part of the essence of the invention; the subject-matter of the patent is the use of the particular ingredients in that particular proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another uses the same ingredients in materially different proportions to produce a similar or better effect, that use may be a new subject-matter and not an infringement. This class of patents requires strict proof that the defendant worked within the specified proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight departures for evasion are fraudulent
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight departure from the specification for the purpose of evasion only would be a fraud upon the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is whether the mode of working by the defendant has been essentially or substantially different; courts look at substance and result, not merely formal differences in steps or wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior utility as a test of non-identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things are not the same under the patent law when one is practically substantially better than the other, and this improvement is not gained by the use of known mechanical equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior practical utility or a materially better result produced by different means can indicate no infringement. But improvement alone does not avoid infringement if the infringing device contains the whole substance of the patented device plus something additional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent stands upon its subject-matter (combination patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent stands upon its subject-matter, and accordingly the question of infringement depends upon the use of that which is covered by the patent. Where a patent is for the combination alone, it is no infringement to use any of the parts or things which go to make up the combination, provided the combination itself be not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent claims solely a particular combination, using individual old parts (even some of them) does not infringe unless the combination as claimed is used. Evidence must show whether the claimed combination is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of material new parts within a combination (English rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid patent for an entire combination for a process gives protection to each part thereof that is new and material to that process, without any express claim of particular parts, notwithstanding that some parts of the combination are old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this view, imitation or pirating of any material part of the invention may constitute an infringement even if the whole combination is not copied. Courts may treat imitation of a material part as actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation/piracy of a material part is an infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention consists of several parts and one part is a very useful invention, the imitation or pirating of any material part of such an invention is an infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If a patentee invents a machine of three parts and a defendant imitates the useful part while substituting other modes for the less useful parts, that may still be infringement; plaintiffs may maintain an action for copying a material part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant has employed a mechanical equivalent as a substitute for some material element of the plaintiff's combination, it will be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must inquire whether the substitute is a known mechanical equivalent. If so, replacing an element by its equivalent does not avoid infringement; examples include equivalent means in loom-stopping mechanisms or welding techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must show invention and that effect was produced as specified
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the patentee brings an action on his patent, if the novelty or effect of the invention be disputed, he must show in what his invention consists, and that he procured the effect proposed, in the manner specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications must be sufficiently precise (showing degrees, quantities, modes). Slight defects in specification may vacate the patent; juries examine evidence on whether defendants followed the specification and whether specified proportions/conditions were essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of separate ingredients or partial combinations is not necessarily infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent describes a combination of ingredients producing a new effect, the use of separate ingredients, or some of them partially combined, will not constitute use of the invention unless the combination (including proportions and arrangements) claimed is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ingredients had been separately used before, or proportions are not essential, then partial or separate use may not infringe. Courts distinguish mere partial use from use of the patented combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-over-form inquiry for jury fact-findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal determination of infringement depends on substance and result — juries decide on the evidence whether defendants' mode of working is in substance the same or essentially different from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony of practical/scientific witnesses and comparisons of materials, proportions, modes, and results are critical. Single witnesses can determine outcomes; inconsistent testimony or lack of proof that defendants used the claimed mode may defeat infringement claims.
